title:
Some personal news. After nearly three years, I stepped away from FRL & Shortcut earlier this month.

In 2023, I dropped out of my mba at MIT to cofound FRL with Robert, Shuying, and Andrew. Cofoundin
content:
Some personal news. After nearly three years, I stepped away from FRL & Shortcut earlier this month.

In 2023, I dropped out of my mba at MIT to cofound FRL with Robert, Shuying, and Andrew. Cofounding a company is all consuming, and they have been the best cofounders I could have ever asked for.

Robert/Shuying never mentioned it again, but I had a pregnant wife at the time and little savings, and Shuying helped cover my bills for months while we were still fundraising. I’ll forever be grateful.

I was a former professional basketball dunker and self-taught dev, suddenly building with MIT professors, phds, and programming medalists.

We immediately built a brand for far-out and inspiring applied research, building the first AI agents that people could play with in Minecraft. We even simulated a civilization of 1,000 agents with Project Sid (I still think this was the most fun / forward looking multi agent work until OpenClaw).

On Oct 22, 2024, Anthropic released the CUA preview and Robert made the call for us to tackle OSWorld. He had the vision to lean into codegen and to build what we called “skills”(!!) to separate the hands from the mind at the time. Shuying set up the infra to run massive parallel evals so we could get dozens of scores a day. We beat SOTA in 1 week and more than doubled it in 5 weeks. It’s a huge regret that we did not open source and publish our research.

We raised a $30M+ Series A less than one month later and went all-in on building CUA inspired products.

Unfortunately, our first two products did not stick at all, and we found ourselves in the hardest chapter of our company history.

At this point, each of the cofounders had performed what felt like mini-miracles except for me (Andrew beat the voyager benchmark with Altera agents!). I felt the enormous weight of the moment, I insisted that i build my own product for us. With a very small team, I built and launched Shortcut… and it made quite an impact. 

I put all of my love and care into Shortcut over the last 18 months. It took some time for our research lab to reorient after launch, but we found our stride soon after. We created an entire ai product (and startup) category and i don’t think it’s an exaggeration to say we changed the way people use Excel. 

Shortcut is growing rapidly (4x in 2026!) and we are live in many of the biggest investment funds in the world. The product has clearly entered its next phase as a scaled product with a killer team at the wheel. 

And with this new chapter, the time has come for me to take a step back after pouring my heart into this company and product. The world looks really different than it did in 2023, and I'm excited to go back to the drawing board.

I’m deeply grateful to my cofounders, teammates (too many of you to name, but thank you for your trust and for carrying the torch forward), investors, customers, and our users. You are in awesome hands.

Most importantly, I’d like to thank my wife, Melanie. 

Thank you for building our family, for your strength, and for your confidence in me that far surpasses my own. You are the reason for anything we accomplish, and the reason any of it at all matters in the end.

Nico

Yesterday Anthropic released a reserach paper. Claude was tasked with improvi
content:
Anthropic just published one of the clearest previews of recursive self-improvement yet. But we still dont talk about it.

Yesterday Anthropic released a reserach paper. Claude was tasked with improving the alignment of other AI models. It searched the literature, proposed methods, created training data, trained the models, evaluated the results and iterated.

It improved all 10 tested alignment failures without degrading measured general capabilities. Anthropic even used the weaker Sonnet 5 to post-train an early Opus 4.8 checkpoint, bringing its alignment close to the released production model within 60 hours.

Anthropic: 

“The best AAR method beats what experienced humans propose, on average within six hours. (...) Human-guided research directions do not lead to stronger performance.”

This is not full recursive self-improvement yet. The improved model did not become the next researcher and repeat the process. But most of the loop now exists:

AI researches AI.
AI trains improved AI.
AI evaluates the result.
AI iterates.
The loop closes when the improved AI becomes the researcher for the next generation. That is when progress could begin to compound. And tbh Id say we are pretty close to it. So talk that reserach serious.

h/t to @tradernewsai for bringing this to my attention

Sources: Anthropic blog / Tech Crunch

title:
New Google paper makes a strong case for replacing ever-growing agent histories with a small, explicit execution state.

Long-horizon agents may need far less conversation history than we give them: t
content:
New Google paper makes a strong case for replacing ever-growing agent histories with a small, explicit execution state.

Long-horizon agents may need far less conversation history than we give them: this paper finds that replacing the growing transcript with explicit current state cuts token use and often improves accuracy.

SKILL.state gives the model only the skill instructions, a structured state, and the latest observation. After each step, the reasoning trace is discarded and only a validated state update survives.

That keeps prompt size roughly constant as the task gets longer.

On a 100-step warehouse task with Gemini-3-Flash, SKILL.state scored 0.94 while using 65,408 tokens. The LangGraph-style baseline scored 0.91 and used 1,062,387 tokens, a 16.2X difference.

The design does have a boundary: it works only when everything needed later can be captured in the state schema.

But starting today, we're establishing a new culture. I pinned the incident report to README, and every single agent is gonna to have to read the entire log every morning before it executes a single token.

content:
Really believe that ADHDs, if they play their cards well, might be the biggest winners of this AI gold rush

Cause unlike corporate careers rewarding consistency & compounding, the new world disproportionally rewards curiosity, obsession, rapid switching and intensity

The basic problem with ADHD in the old world was that curiosity was expensive. You’d get obsessed with some random idea, spend 3 days learning everything about it, want to build something, then realise you need 6 months to learn how to code / design / whatever (or pay someone who can) and eventually move onto the next thing

But AI completely changes that equation because the distance between “wait this would be cool” and actually testing it has collapsed from months to sometimes hours. You can get curious about some niche industry in the morning, understand the basics by lunch, vibe code something in the afternoon and potentially have people testing it that evening. So this disproportionately rewards people whose natural state is basically jumping between rabbit holes, connecting unrelated things and occasionally becoming insanely obsessed with one of them

AI is also slowly deleting the boring middle. A lot of ADHD people aren’t necessarily bad at starting things or going insanely deep when something captures their attention, they’re bad at the 200 repetitive steps between “this is exciting” and “this is finished” (boilerplate, formatting, basic debugging, admin, iteration, etc.) And those are increasingly exactly the things you can delegate to AI, which means the economic value of being insanely curious + occasionally obsessive probably goes up, while the cost of being bad at repetitive execution goes down

But there’s a massive catch, because AI is also creating the greatest distraction machine ever invented. Every morning there’s a new model, agent, tool, business model or “once in a generation opportunity” to chase, and the same brain that benefits most from cheap experimentation is also the one most likely to spend 5 years being extremely early to everything and compounding absolutely nothing

So the actual winning combination might actually be ADHD-style exploration + artificially imposed constraints: explore aggressively, follow weird rabbit holes, test way more things than a normal person would, but once something works force yourself into sprints where you’re simply not allowed to play another game

For most of history the economy disproportionately rewarded people who could reliably do the same useful thing for 8 hours a day, 250 days a year. For this weird period of AI, the returns temporarily shift towards people who can obsess over 20 things, connect 2 that nobody else connected, then disappear for 3 days and build the thing

content:
Every AI coding agent already reads your codebase.

What if it could understand every dependency before making changes?

Inside every codebase is a structure: functions call other functions, files import other files, changes ripple through the system. That structure is not hidden. It is just relationships that any graph can map and any agent can query.

There is an open-source tool that turns codebases into knowledge graphs that AI agents can query. It runs entirely in your browser. It is called GitNexus.

It started in August 2025 when developers built a client-side knowledge graph creator that indexes repositories without sending code to servers. Drop in a GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps repo or ZIP file. Get an interactive knowledge graph with a built-in Graph RAG agent. Works with 21 programming languages.

Here is what happens when you use GitNexus.

You run npx gitnexus analyze in your repository. It indexes every file, function, class, and dependency. It builds a knowledge graph that tracks every relationship. Connect your coding agent with npx gitnexus setup. Now your agent can query the graph through MCP tools.

The problem it solves: AI agents edit code without knowing what depends on it. Agent changes UserService validate function. Doesn't know 47 functions depend on its return type. Breaking changes ship.

GitNexus precomputes structure at index time. Clustering. Tracing. Scoring. When your agent asks what depends on UserService, it gets a complete answer in one query. Eight callers. Three clusters. All with confidence scores. No multi-step exploration needed.

A team measured impact on code reliability. AI agent without GitNexus: 3 breaking changes per 10 edits because it missed downstream dependencies. Same agent with GitNexus MCP integration: zero breaking changes because it checked impact before editing.

Two ways to use it.

CLI plus MCP for daily development. Index repos locally. Connect Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, or Windsurf through MCP. Query the graph from your editor. Check impact before changes. Full repos, any size.

Web UI for quick exploration. No install needed.
Upload a repository or paste a GitHub URL. Explore the graph visually. Chat with the built-in Graph RAG agent. Runs entirely in browser with LadybugDB WASM.

The graph shows more than connections. Community clustering groups related code. Execution flow traces how data moves. Call chains map function dependencies. Risk scores identify fragile areas. All computed at index time, not query time.

MCP tools for agents. Impact analysis shows what breaks when you change a function. Dependency trace reveals who calls your code. Architecture view maps domains and boundaries. Execution flow follows data through the system. Change risk scores affected files.

Works with 21 languages. TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin, Dart, Vue, HTML, CSS, Shell, PowerShell, Dockerfile, Jinja.

Tree-sitter parsing with native and WASM backends. LadybugDB for graph storage. Native version for CLI with persistence. WASM version for browser with in-memory storage. Bridge mode connects them: web UI can browse CLI-indexed repos.

One command setup. Analyze creates the graph, installs agent skills, registers hooks, and writes context files. Setup configures MCP so agents can query the graph. Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and other MCP-compatible editors.

Optional embedding support for semantic search. Deploy to Render with one click for team access. Self-hosted backend mode for unlimited scale. Access control with token authentication.

46.3k+ stars on GitHub. Created August 2025. Active development with new language support and agent integrations.

Every codebase already has structure.

GitNexus maps it so agents can see before they change.

content:
Every video production already takes hours of work.

What if your AI coding assistant could handle the entire pipeline?

Inside every video project is a workflow: research the topic, write the script, generate assets, edit the timeline, compose the final video. That workflow is not locked behind expensive software. It is just tasks that any agent with the right tools can execute.

There is an open-source agentic video production system that turns coding assistants into video studios. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, and Codex. It is called OpenMontage.

It started in March 2026 when a developer named Calesthio built a system that connects 12 production pipelines, 100+ tools, and 700+ agent skill files. Describe what you want in plain language. Your agent handles research, scripting, asset generation, editing, and final composition. AGPL licensed.

Here is what happens when you use OpenMontage.

You tell your coding assistant to make a 60-second explainer about neural networks. The agent researches the topic with live web search. Writes the script with narrative structure. Generates AI images for visuals or retrieves real stock footage from open archives. Records narration with voice direction. Finds royalty-free background music automatically. Burns in word-level subtitles. Renders the final video.

The distinction: OpenMontage can make real video from actual motion clips, not just animated stills. The agent builds a corpus from free stock footage and open archives. Retrieves actual motion clips. Edits them into a timeline. Renders a finished piece.

A creator tracked production costs. The Last Banana: 60-second Pixar-style animated short. Six Kling v3 motion clips via fal. Google Chirp3-HD narration. Royalty-free piano music. TikTok-style captions. Remotion composition. Total cost: 1 dollar and 33 cents.

Reimagine Your Universe: 50-second vertical transformation film. Five generated motion scenes. Sparse narration. Pixabay score. HyperFrames composition. Total cost: about 4 dollars.

How Salt Made History: 100-second cinematic documentary. Real-world footage woven with original narration and hand-authored motion graphics. Etched titles. Etymology reveals. Animated maps. Historical timeline. All from one prompt.

It includes 12 production pipelines.

Cinematic documentary. Animated explainer. Product showcase. Vertical social content. Stock montage editor. Music video. Educational series. Reference-based remakes. Documentary research. 3D world builder. Image-to-video animation. Real footage retrieval and editing.

Backlot living storyboard shows production progress. Chat tells you what the agent said. Backlot shows what the production is actually doing. Stages light up as pipeline runs. Script lands as screenplay page. Scene cards update while assets generate. Every provider decision and cost displayed. Opens automatically when production starts.

Asset generation approval gates. Production pauses on scene-by-scene contact sheet. Shows takes, prompts, per-asset cost, quality scores. You approve visuals before render, not after. Creative gates hold until you respond in chat.

Start from reference videos. Paste a YouTube video, Short, Reel, TikTok, or local clip. Agent analyzes transcript, pacing, scenes, keyframes, and style. You get 2 to 3 differentiated concepts, honest tool path, cost estimates, and sample before full production.

Multi-point self-review system. FFprobe validation. Frame sampling. Audio level analysis. Delivery promise verification. Subtitle checks. Every provider selection scored across 7 dimensions with auditable decision log.

Works with multiple AI coding assistants. Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Codex. Open the project in your assistant and describe what you want. The agent handles the entire production.

Supports multiple generation providers. Flux, Stable Diffusion, Kling, Veo, Luma, Runway, Pika for video. ElevenLabs, Google Chirp for narration. Pixabay, Pexels for royalty-free music and stock footage. Remotion for composition and rendering.

Requires Python 3.10+, FFmpeg, and Node.js 18+. Clone repo, run make setup, open in your coding assistant, describe your video. The system handles research, asset generation, editing, and final render.

53.9k+ stars on GitHub. Created March 2026. AGPL licensed. Active development.

(Google and Microsoft are betting on the same one.)

content:
Agents reach websites in 6 ways.

(Google and Microsoft are betting on the same one.)

Ask an agent to buy something and watch it work. It screenshots the page, looks for something shaped like a button, clicks, and screenshots again to see what happened.

You pay tokens every time it looks, and one redesign breaks the run.

The site already knows what it can do. It has a search, a cart, a checkout, and none of that is written down anywhere a program can read.

Here are the six, ordered from furthest from the interface to closest.

1) Raw API. Your script calls the backend with a key you manage. Precise and fast, though you had to find the endpoints yourself and the website never enters the picture.

2) Backend MCP server. The company describes its actions as named tools and your agent connects to them. Someone who understands the product wrote those definitions, so they name real actions instead of guessed ones. The interface is still skipped.

3) Computer use. The agent sees the live page as an image and clicks around it. Nothing to configure, but every look costs money and a layout change confuses it.

4) Browser automation over the DOM. The agent reads the page's underlying code instead of a picture of it. More reliable than pixels, except the tooling is generic, so the agent still infers meaning from anonymous divs and unlabeled buttons.

5) WebMCP, the one Chrome and Edge are building together. The page declares its own actions with names, plain-English descriptions, and typed inputs, and your agent calls them inside your live browser session.

6) The site's built-in assistant. The company ships a chat box, picks the model, and pays for the tokens. It works, and it is not your agent, so nothing it learns about you carries anywhere else.

Three things vary across the six. Whose agent does the work, what you configure before anything happens, and what the agent receives when it arrives.

Every option except one gives up at least one of the three. Raw API and backend MCP hand you typed actions and remove the website. Computer use asks for no setup and hands over pixels. The built-in assistant is precise and belongs to the vendor.

WebMCP is the only one that keeps all three. Your own agent, nothing to configure, and named actions instead of guesswork.

Banger paper from Apple.

It's actually a really neat idea that's easy to implement. And it showcases the awesomeness of MCP.

Agent Seer starts from a single MCP spec and synthesizes multi-turn agent test scenarios with no examples, no live tool access, and no domain-specific tuning.

Function names, natural-language descriptions and typed parameter schemas already carry enough semantics to generate graded scenarios with synthetic tool outputs, which then expand into mock-data-grounded dialogues.

Hand-built agent benchmarks demand deep domain expertise, do not scale across tool ecosystems, and go stale as soon as an API changes. Generating them from the live spec keeps pace with the ecosystem instead.

They ran it on seven MCP specifications spanning different domains and suite sizes, with complete tool coverage on small and medium specs.

Parameter schema complexity predicts quality variation far better than tool-suite size does. And argument value accuracy is the dominant failure mode, a sub-dimension that coarse name-match tool-calling metrics cannot see at all.

Six weeks is enough to get certified as a Claude Architect if you follow the order and do not skip ahead.

Week 1 is coursework only: Building with the Claude API, Introduction to Model Context Protocol, Claude Code in Action, Claude 101. Skipping this step is how people show up to the exam knowing prompts but not the system underneath them.

Week 2 turns that coursework into real projects using Claude Code, the Agent SDK, the Anthropic API, and MCP. Reading about a tool and building with it are not the same skill, and the exam tests the second one.

Week 3 shifts from building to the exam itself: go through all six exam scenarios, get familiar with the five domains, and learn exactly which skills each task assessment is checking for.

Week 4 is where the real preparation happens. Build a multi-tool agent with escalation logic, configure Claude Code for a team development workflow, build a structured data extraction pipeline, and design and debug a multi-agent research pipeline. These four exercises mirror what the actual exam asks for.

Week 5 is a practice exam. Aim for a score above 850 out of 1000 before moving on.

Week 6 is the real exam, and you only get one attempt.

content:
Stateful vs. Stateless MCP core.

(Anthropic's biggest MCP update)

Let us explain what that means:

Until this release, talking to an MCP server worked like a phone call. Both sides ran an initialize handshake, and the server returned a session id carried on every later request.

That session was a live object inside one specific server process, holding the negotiated state.

Picture a restaurant where the waiter who took the order is the only one who knows what was ordered. Everything works until that waiter goes home.

Because that state lives in one process, a balancer could not spread requests across three MCP server instances. Teams pinned clients with sticky sessions or pushed session state into shared storage, which blocked autoscaling and made a single restart drop every open session.

The latest update deletes all of it. The handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone, and each request now carries its own protocol version, client identity, and capabilities in a _meta field.

Clients that want the capability list up front can call server/discover, but nothing requires it.

That flips the restaurant around. Every request is a written order slip now, and any waiter can fill it.

So any request can land on any instance behind a plain round-robin balancer, with no shared session store. MCP servers become ordinary HTTP services that run on serverless and edge, and survive restarts.

Removing sessions broke three features, so each got rebuilt.

→ Tools that need to ask the user something mid-call used to push that request down a held-open stream. Now the server returns input_required and the client retries with the answers attached.

→ Method and tool names moved into the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers, so a gateway or rate limiter can route and meter without parsing the JSON-RPC body.

→ List responses carry ttlMs and cacheScope, so clients cache tool catalogs instead of refetching them on every reconnect.

State did not disappear here, it moved somewhere the model can see it.

Applications that need continuity mint an explicit handle from a tool and have the model pass it back as an argument on the next call.

A session id in a header is invisible to the model, while a handle in the arguments is something it can read, thread between tools, and recover from after a failed call.

Official Spec: https://t.co/rJJZIoEoya

Since we are on MCP, we also wrote about why the MCP versus CLI debate was the wrong one, and how agents can call tools by writing code instead of loading every schema into context.

The article is quoted below.

attention is not a data structure
rag is not a knowledge graph
a bigger window is not linking

▹ why the flat window cooks you

everything in that llm prompt is flat
kimi k3 re-derives every relationship
on every single api call · token burn on loop

import graphs · call graphs · type graphs
schemas · tickets · prs · config edges
none of that survives as structure

claude · cursor · kimi all hit the same wall
when the hop count goes past one

▹ graph vs context window

a knowledge graph stores the edge once
pay for entity extraction one time
then traverse hops for free

the scale math is unforgiving
and it hits different once you see it

100 entities = 4,950 possible pairs
1,000 entities = 499,500 candidates
10k entities = ~50 million pairwise checks

no context window holds that graph
it holds a repo dump and prays
that entity links fall out of kimi k3

▹ entity resolution is the real boss

naive string matching lands near 70%
on real corpora and production codebases

70% over two hops is 49%
three hops is 34% accuracy

your rag retrieval looked clean
your answer failed at ingest
not at query time

coreference · aliasing · rename drift
same service · three string labels
one wrong merge and the path is cooked

▹ the cost stack that actually prints

cheap blocking keys first
embeddings + vector search second
ann / cosine only on the shortlist

kimi k3 only on ambiguous pairs
usually under 5% of candidates

that is the whole cost structure
moonshot pricing earns its keep there

burn frontier tokens on the hard 5%
not on every pairwise check in the repo

most people still paste the whole tree
into a million-token prompt and hope

winners extract once · resolve hard cases
then walk the graph like infrastructure

▹ the take

count the entities in your knowledge graph
then count the ones you actually meant

the gap is your real accuracy
not the kimi k3 context window flex

the edge is not more tokens
the edge is the edges

The proposed shutoff date is November 12, 2026, which OpenAI said is the maximum notice its custom agreement allows. In an August 28 statement, the company said it wants developers to retain access as long as the contract permits, while refusing to provide future models to Cursor.

OpenAI called the choice “incredibly tough,” but said it cannot be confident SpaceX will use its technology within its terms of service, citing experience with Elon Musk’s companies violating contracts.

content:
GPT-5.6 Sol is DUMBER than Fable 5.

As a big supporter of Sol, OpenAI’s latest model, I’m no longer satisfied with its performance.

That said, its performance issues seem to be caused by the complexity of the harness the OpenAI team is currently building.

The problem has become obvious to everyone by now.

I’m talking about subagent orchestration.

When you assign a task to CODEX using subagents, the result is genuinely poor.

GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra cannot even manage subagents properly, so there is a major underlying issue that needs to be solved, especially ahead of the Astra release.

On the other hand, when I let Fable handle the orchestration of GPT-5.6 Sol without subagents, the resulting output is significantly better.

I really hope Tibo reads this feedback, because this issue has never truly been solved since subagents were first introduced.

For this reason, as things stand today, GPT models are more worthwhile to use through Cursor or other harnesses.

content:
Everyone talks about how much compute AI needs.

But for Physical AI, I think the bigger problem is much simpler:

Where does the training data come from?

LLMs had the entire internet to learn from. Robots don't have that luxury.

A robot learning to grasp an object, pour water, or navigate a space needs physical action data that captures how movement actually happens in the real world.

And collecting that data manually is expensive and difficult to scale.

This is where @axisrobotics takes an interesting approach.

Instead of putting every human operator beside expensive physical hardware, Axis turns robot training into a browser based game.

You connect, control a virtual robotic arm, complete tasks, and generate verified action trajectories.

The interesting part is that the game isn't just entertainment.

The interaction becomes data.

Axis uses simulation because it can make training more scalable while avoiding many of the cost, safety, privacy, and uptime limitations of collecting everything directly in the physical world.

And there's another important distinction:

Video can show a robot moving, but it doesn't necessarily capture the underlying physical information needed for action  things like poses, contacts, and forces.

So the problem isn't simply making robots smarter.

It's creating enough high quality physical-action data for them to learn from.

That's the problem Axis is trying to attack.

Better data → better training → more capable robots.

Sleepagotchi: From "Sleep-to-Earn" to "Sleep-to-Understand" @sleepagotchi 

Sleepagotchi is gradually evolving into a product quite different from what many initially envisioned. Yet, upon closer insp
content:
Sleepagotchi: From "Sleep-to-Earn" to "Sleep-to-Understand" @sleepagotchi 

Sleepagotchi is gradually evolving into a product quite different from what many initially envisioned. Yet, upon closer inspection, this shift resembles an evolution rather than a sudden pivot.
The initial foundation: gamifying sleep
Sleepagotchi’s original concept was straightforward: sleep better, maintain consistency, and get rewarded for it. 

The "sleep-to-earn" mechanism and gamification elements transformed a nightly, silent activity into something interactive and motivating. This identity was what first brought the project into the public eye.

A greater opportunity lies in data
However, beneath the gaming layer lay a far greater opportunity: data. Every night of sleep generates a multitude of signals duration, timing, consistency, recovery, and behavioral patterns. While wearables are increasingly adept at capturing these signals, data collection is not the same as data comprehension.

For instance, a smartwatch might report that you slept for 6 hours and 40 minutes. That figure alone reveals little. The real question is: what does it mean for your specific health, energy levels, or lifestyle habits? This is the gap Sleepagotchi is now targeting.
The shift: building an intelligence layer for the wellness industry

Starting in May 2026, the project began repositioning itself around a broader vision: becoming an "intelligence layer" for the entire wellness economy. In other words, sleep data transforms into context; context becomes personalized insights; and, in the long run, those insights can translate into specific recommendations, habits, or actions for the user. This represents a product scope far broader than simply displaying a sleep score each morning.

It is not about abandoning the original identity, but rather adding a new layer.
Notably, the original identity need not disappear for the new model to function. 

Game mechanics continue to drive engagement, characters keep the experience entertaining, and rewards encourage consistency. All these elements now serve as the front-end interface for a deeper, intelligent system operating in the background.

Therefore, it is more accurate to describe the evolution of Sleepagotchi not as discarding its old identity, but as building upon that foundation: first, getting users interested in their sleep, and then helping them understand what their health data is actually telling them. And quite possibly, this second aspect is the more important one in the long run.

content:
Axis's Simulation Leverage 🧩

Teaching a robot a new task usually takes dozens, sometimes hundreds, of real demonstrations. That's expensive and slow.

@axisrobotics builds a digital twin of the real workspace. Contributors generate task aligned data in simulation and when combined with a small number of real demonstrations, the policy's ability to reach the object jumps significantly. That data then turns into a Booster specific foundation prior, so the next task needs even less real data.

The numbers back this up: with just 10 real demonstrations, the robot made zero contact with the object across 20 trials. Add 50 simulation trajectories to those same 10 demonstrations and contact jumps to 17/20. Overall, the simulation real mixture improved lift rates by up to 10 percentage points over real only training.

The foundation model side shows striking results too: zero shot wrist to target distance dropped from 17.27 cm to 5.78 cm, and non target arm movement was cut by 95%. A foundation model trained on just 30 demonstrations even outperformed the original model trained on 60.

Axis Robotics keeps running this loop alongside its data layer on @base as well.

The interesting part is that MHS is trying to solve a problem people don’t tal
content:
Just read about Anthropic’s Model Hardware Standard (MHS) and this feels much bigger than another AI integration update.

The interesting part is that MHS is trying to solve a problem people don’t talk about enough: AI can reason, but most physical machines still speak completely different languages.

A microscope, liquid handler, robotic arm or quantum lab setup can each have their own software, APIs and operating rules. 

Connecting them can take weeks or months of custom engineering.

MHS is basically trying to create a common language between AI agents and physical hardware.

The driver gives an agent information about what a machine can do, what it is measuring, and what safety limits exist.

Then the agent can use MCP, CLI or APIs to control multiple devices and coordinate them together.

The laser example is what really caught my attention.

Claude could adjust a laser, look at the camera result, make another adjustment, learn from the process and eventually turn what it learned into a deterministic script.

That is a very different AI workflow.

It’s not just:
AI → answer

It becomes:
AI → observe → act → learn → automate
And the early ecosystem is already interesting with AWS, Tecan, QIAGEN, Universal Robots, Doosan Robotics, Raspberry Pi, Hugging Face, Danaher and others exploring MHS.

My opinion: if MHS actually becomes an open standard, it could become an important infrastructure layer for AI-native laboratories and factories

But I think the biggest challenge isn't getting AI to control machines.

It's making sure AI knows when it should NOT control them.

Physical mistakes are different from software mistakes. A wrong parameter can destroy a sample, damage equipment or create a real safety issue.

That’s why the safety work during this research preview may end up being just as important as the standard itself.

AI agents are moving from screens into the physical world.

MHS could be one of the bridges.

Your phone number has become much more than a way for someone to call you, and @BeldexCoin is challenging the idea that a phone number should automatically be the foundation of your digital identity. That's one reason BChat caught my attention. Instead of requiring a phone number or email address to create an account, it uses BChat IDs for communication. The idea is simple but important: communicating with someone shouldn't automatically require attaching your real-world identity to the conversation. �
BChat +1
What makes this even more interesting is that BChat isn't only focused on encrypting the words inside a conversation. Beldex's privacy model also looks at the metadata surrounding communication, because information such as activity patterns can reveal things even when the actual message content is protected. �
BChat
I think this is where the privacy conversation gets deeper. The future isn't necessarily about disappearing from the internet. It's about being able to participate without every interaction being permanently tied to a real-world identifier. If Web3 is about giving users more control, choosing how your digital identity is represented should be part of that control.

title:
🚨🚨🚨 Remember how Ripple has been positioning ripple:native for this for years? 

Mike Novogratz just described the kind of Treasury stress that could make that positioning matter more than ever.

What
content:
🚨🚨🚨 Remember how Ripple has been positioning ripple:native for this for years? 

Mike Novogratz just described the kind of Treasury stress that could make that positioning matter more than ever.

What Mike Novogratz was talking about at SALT was not talking about some random crypto cycle.

He was talking about the foundation of the financial system.

Long-dated U.S. Treasuries.

The risk is simple to understand even if you never trade bonds.

If investors start losing confidence in long-term U.S. government debt, yields can rise, liquidity can weaken and policymakers can be forced to support the long end of the Treasury market much more aggressively.

That is the setup Novogratz was pointing toward.

And when I started connecting that scenario with what Ripple has quietly been building around ripple:native, XRPL, RLUSD, collateral, tokenization and institutional liquidity, the bigger picture started looking very different.

Because the important question is not:

“What happens to crypto if Treasury yields move?”

The better question is:

“What kind of financial infrastructure becomes more valuable when the biggest institutions in the world suddenly care even more about liquidity, collateral and moving capital efficiently?”

That question leads straight into what Ripple has spent years building.

And Treasury is already moving.

On August 19, 2026, the U.S. Treasury announced that it would at least double the maximum size of its long-end liquidity-support buybacks from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation beginning September 9.

The focus is directly on 10–20 year and 20–30 year Treasuries.

Treasury's stated purpose is to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors.

Read that carefully.

Greater liquidity support.

That is not something I brush off as another bond-market headline.

Liquidity is the blood of the financial system.

You can own billions of dollars of valuable assets, but if you cannot move them, finance them, settle them or use them where they are needed at the right time, you still have a problem.

That is why Mike Novogratz's SALT discussion matters so much to me.

He is pointing toward a situation where the financial system could be forced to care much more about the efficiency of the underlying plumbing.

And Ripple has been positioning itself around that plumbing for years.

People still associate Ripple primarily with cross-border payments.

I think that view is already outdated.

Payments are still there.

But look at what is being assembled around them now.

Tokenized assets.

FX.

Institutional liquidity.

Collateral.

Credit.

Prime brokerage.

Stablecoin liquidity.

Custody.

Onchain settlement.

Lending.

Programmable assets.

24/7 financial infrastructure.

That is no longer one payment product.

It is becoming a stack.

And Treasury stress could make every part of that stack more relevant.

Here is the easiest way I can explain why.

Imagine you own a house worth $1 million.

You are wealthy on paper.

But you suddenly need $100,000 immediately and your wealth is locked inside that house.

The house still has value.

Your problem is access.

Now scale that problem up to institutions holding billions in Treasuries, securities, cash, currencies and other financial assets.

A bank can have enormous assets and still need liquidity somewhere else.

A hedge fund can own high-quality collateral and still need to move that collateral quickly.

A prime broker can have counterparties demanding margin.

A derivatives venue can require collateral immediately.

A market maker can need cash in one market while its assets are sitting somewhere else.

That is what liquidity pressure looks like in the real world.

The problem is often not the absence of value.

The problem is getting value to the right place fast enough.

That is why collateral mobility matters.

And Ripple made a move in August 2026 that suddenly looks much more important when you put it beside Mike Novogratz's Treasury scenario.

Ripple invested in ZILO and Licuido.

Those investments expand regulated issuance, transfer agency and collateral mobility across Ripple infrastructure and XRPL.

Collateral mobility sounds like one of those phrases people skip past.

I do not.

Because if long-duration Treasury markets become unstable, collateral becomes one of the most important things in the room.

Banks need it.

Clearing houses need it.

Prime brokers need it.

Repo markets need it.

Derivatives venues need it.

Liquidity providers need it.

Institutions need to know not only how much collateral they have, but how quickly they can mobilize it.

That is a huge difference.

And tokenization can change that equation.

A Treasury inside traditional securities infrastructure is valuable.

A tokenized Treasury that can move through digital infrastructure, settle against tokenized cash and potentially participate in credit markets becomes more flexible.

Same economic asset.

Different plumbing.

That is what interests me.

Tokenization does not have to reinvent the Treasury.

It can reinvent what institutions are able to do with the Treasury.

Transfer it around the clock.

Move it between counterparties.

Use it as collateral.

Settle it against digital cash.

Integrate it into lending infrastructure.

Make it programmable.

Reduce the amount of time capital spends waiting between systems.

That becomes extremely valuable when liquidity is under pressure.

And XRPL is being built directly into that world.

Ripple's institutional roadmap already identifies Treasuries, money-market funds, stablecoins and private credit as assets that increasingly need onchain credit and collateral infrastructure.

That is why I keep saying the XRP story is getting much bigger than payments.

Imagine the traditional financial system as hundreds of pools of money separated by walls.

There is dollar liquidity.

Treasury collateral.

Foreign currencies.

Funds.

Credit.

Derivatives collateral.

Stablecoins.

Bank deposits.

Each market can be deep on its own.

The problem starts when value needs to move between them.

That movement costs time.

It can require multiple intermediaries.

It can require pre-funded capital.

It can depend on settlement windows.

It can leave capital sitting idle.

Ripple's strategy increasingly looks like an attempt to make those walls thinner.

XRPL becomes the rail.

RLUSD becomes tokenized dollar liquidity.

Tokenized Treasuries become digital collateral.

Ripple Prime connects institutional liquidity, credit and settlement.

Ripple Mint gives institutions direct tools for managing RLUSD liquidity.

The XRPL Lending Protocol creates the path toward onchain credit.

ZILO and Licuido push the infrastructure further into issuance and collateral mobility.

Then you have ripple:native sitting natively inside the ledger.

Not as a dollar.

Not as a Treasury.

Not as a bank deposit.

As liquidity.

That distinction is the entire thesis for me.

RLUSD can represent dollars.

A tokenized Treasury can represent government debt.

A foreign stablecoin can represent another currency.

Private credit can represent a completely different financial claim.

Those assets do not need XRP to become what they already are.

XRP becomes interesting when they need to interact.

Suppose an institution holds tokenized Treasuries but needs tokenized dollars.

Suppose another institution holds RLUSD but needs exposure to a foreign currency.

Suppose one market has deep liquidity and another does not.

Every combination does not automatically have an enormous direct market.

That is exactly why bridge liquidity exists.

Ripple describes XRP as the auto-bridge asset inside XRPL environments where it can help connect liquidity between different assets.

So instead of looking at XRP as one more thing being traded, I look at what happens if it becomes useful between things being traded.

That is a very different position.

Tokenized Treasury → XRP → RLUSD.

RLUSD → XRP → foreign stablecoin.

Tokenized collateral → XRP liquidity → another institutional asset.

Those paths do not mean every transaction must use XRP.

That is not even the most interesting part.

What matters is what happens as the number of assets and liquidity pools grows.

More tokenized assets create more markets.

More markets create more pairs.

More pairs create more fragmented liquidity.

Fragmented liquidity creates a stronger reason for efficient bridge assets.

That is the network effect I care about.

Then Mike Novogratz's SALT scenario becomes even more important.

Because if confidence in the long end weakens enough, policymakers do not simply watch.

The Federal Reserve has historically used maturity-extension programs such as Operation Twist, selling shorter-term securities and buying longer-term Treasuries to push down long-term yields and loosen financial conditions.

Fed Vice Chair Bowman has also said a similar maturity-extension strategy remains conceptually available as a balance-sheet tool.

Now picture what that environment means.

Treasury is supporting liquidity through larger long-end buybacks.

The Federal Reserve has tools designed to influence the long end.

Financial institutions start becoming even more sensitive to duration.

Funding becomes more expensive.

Cash buffers become more important.

Collateral availability becomes more important.

Liquidity ratios become more important.

Balance-sheet efficiency becomes more important.

And suddenly the old habit of keeping large pools of capital sitting around the world becomes increasingly painful.

That lands directly on Ripple's original XRP proposition.

Ripple has spent years talking about a model where institutions can access liquidity dynamically instead of maintaining fully funded pools across every jurisdiction.

That matters because pre-funded liquidity is capital that cannot be used somewhere else.

When money is cheap and liquidity is everywhere, inefficiency can survive for a long time.

When liquidity becomes expensive, people start looking for every dollar they can free.

That is why I find this setup so bullish.

The financial system does not need another asset simply sitting there.

It needs assets and infrastructure that help capital work harder.

XRP's value proposition has always been tied to moving liquidity instead of trapping it.

Now look at Ripple Prime.

This might be one of the most overlooked parts of the whole story.

Ripple now operates a global institutional prime-brokerage business.

Ripple Prime provides credit intermediation, collateral management, net settlement, institutional liquidity and digital asset execution.

Those words become much more important during bond-market stress.

Credit.

Collateral.

Settlement.

Liquidity.

Counterparty management.

Those are the pressure points.

So Ripple today is positioned in a very different way from the Ripple people remember from earlier XRP cycles.

Ripple Prime sits directly in institutional capital markets.

XRPL sits underneath as digital settlement infrastructure.

That gives Ripple exposure to both sides of the problem.

Institutions need financing and liquidity.

Assets need somewhere efficient to settle.

Then RLUSD adds another layer.

Ripple now has its own tokenized dollar liquidity.

Through Ripple Mint, institutions can mint, redeem, access and programmatically manage RLUSD.

And Ripple is positioning RLUSD around institutional payments, trading, treasury operations and settlement.

Think about the combination now.

A tokenized Treasury represents collateral.

RLUSD represents dollar liquidity.

XRP represents neutral bridge liquidity.

XRPL represents settlement.

Ripple Prime provides institutional market access, financing and collateral management.

XRPL Lending Protocol introduces credit.

That starts resembling an actual financial market.

Not a crypto experiment.

A financial market.

The XRPL Lending Protocol is especially important here because Ripple is building it so assets including Treasuries, money-market funds, stablecoins, commodities and private credit can move beyond simply existing onchain.

They can become part of credit markets.

That changes what tokenization means.

A Treasury that is simply represented by a token is useful.

A Treasury that can move, settle, become collateral and participate in lending is much more powerful.

It becomes productive financial infrastructure.

And if the Treasury market itself becomes one of the major sources of stress in global finance, making Treasury collateral more useful becomes a serious opportunity.

This is why I see Treasury stress potentially accelerating tokenization instead of slowing it down.

Markets change fastest when inefficiencies become painful.

Settlement delays can be tolerated until liquidity is tight.

Fragmented collateral can be tolerated until institutions need it immediately.

Capital trapped between systems can be tolerated until funding costs rise.

Restricted settlement windows can be tolerated until institutions are operating in markets that never stop.

Pressure forces institutions to look harder at the plumbing.

And that is the exact category Ripple is moving into.

Now take Mike Novogratz's SALT warning to the extreme bullish end.

Confidence in long-duration Treasuries gets hit.

Thirty-year yields rise sharply.

Liquidity deteriorates.

Treasury expands buybacks well beyond the new $4 billion maximum.

The Federal Reserve responds with long-duration purchases or an Operation-Twist-style program aimed at the long end.

Treasury issuance shifts toward shorter maturities.

Banks, hedge funds, asset managers and prime brokers become obsessed with duration, funding, cash and collateral.

At the same time, Wall Street accelerates Treasury tokenization because institutions want government collateral that can move 24/7.

Now imagine a bank holding $5 billion of tokenized Treasuries.

It suddenly needs dollar liquidity.

In the old world, that can involve multiple institutions, different settlement layers and time.

In a tokenized environment, the collateral can move through digital infrastructure.

Onchain credit can be accessed.

RLUSD can provide tokenized dollar liquidity.

XRP can route liquidity between assets or counterparties where bridge liquidity is needed.

The collateral can move to another institution.

That is the point where XRPL stops looking like a payment rail.

It starts looking like a collateral network.

Now multiply that bank by the entire institutional market.

Hedge funds.

Asset managers.

Prime brokers.

Banks.

Market makers.

Payment companies.

Exchanges.

Tokenized asset platforms.

Each one needs liquidity.

Each one owns different assets.

Each one has different collateral.

Each one deals in different currencies.

Each one has different counterparties.

And suddenly the real opportunity is not simply sending XRP faster.

The opportunity is connecting liquidity across a tokenized financial system.

That is the outcome that changes how I think about XRP valuation.

Most people still think in crypto terms.

How many retail buyers?

How much speculation?

How much exchange volume?

How much hype?

I am thinking about a different question.

How deep does XRP liquidity need to become if institutions actually start using it as a bridge between tokenized markets?

Because institutional liquidity cannot operate through tiny markets.

If the transaction size grows, the liquidity underneath it has to grow.

Market makers need larger inventories.

Liquidity providers commit more capital.

Institutional XRP markets deepen.

More dollar value needs to be represented by the XRP available for liquidity.

That is the connection between infrastructure and valuation.

XRP does not need to equal the total value of every Treasury or stablecoin moving through XRPL.

It needs enough depth to efficiently bridge the fraction of institutional flows that uses XRP-mediated liquidity.

But imagine the scale if XRPL someday processes trillions of dollars across tokenized Treasuries, FX, stablecoins, payments, credit and collateral.

Even a fraction of those flows would require XRP markets dramatically deeper than the markets people are used to today.

That is why the finite liquidity piece matters.

More value needing to move through available XRP liquidity means each unit can represent more dollar liquidity.

That is what gets me excited about the bigger picture.

Mike Novogratz is talking about stress developing around one of the most important markets on Earth.

Treasury is already increasing long-end liquidity-support buybacks.

The Federal Reserve has historically used tools such as Operation Twist.

Fed Vice Chair Bowman has said maturity extension remains conceptually available.

Ripple, meanwhile, is building around collateral mobility through ZILO and Licuido.

It has Ripple Prime inside institutional credit, collateral and liquidity.

It has RLUSD providing tokenized dollar liquidity.

It has Ripple Mint for programmable RLUSD management.

It has XRPL for settlement.

It has the XRPL Lending Protocol being developed around Treasuries, money-market funds, stablecoins, commodities and private credit.

And it has ripple:native sitting in the middle as native bridge liquidity.

That is why I do not look at Mike Novogratz's SALT comments and think:

“Good for crypto.”

That is way too shallow.

I look at them and think:

If the Treasury market forces the financial system to rethink liquidity, collateral and capital efficiency, Ripple has spent years building directly into the problems that institutions will care about most.

The old system can have valuable assets trapped behind slow movement.

Ripple is building toward valuable assets that can move.

The old system can require capital to sit pre-funded.

XRP is built around accessing liquidity dynamically.

The old system separates collateral, settlement, credit and FX across different pieces of infrastructure.

XRPL is moving toward an environment where those pieces can increasingly interact.

The old system runs through layers of brokers, custodians, clearing houses, banks, payment networks and correspondent relationships.

Ripple is building toward tokenized assets meeting tokenized money through blockchain settlement, liquidity and credit.

That is why I have stayed so deep on ripple:native.

Ripple spent years positioning XRP around liquidity before liquidity became the headline.

Now Mike Novogratz is talking at SALT about a scenario where confidence in long-duration Treasuries can become a major macro problem.

Treasury itself is increasing support for long-end liquidity.

And Ripple is sitting there with an increasingly complete institutional stack built around moving value when liquidity matters most.

If tokenized Treasuries become major collateral…

If RLUSD becomes institutional tokenized cash…

If Ripple Prime connects institutions to financing and liquidity…

If XRPL becomes a settlement layer for tokenized markets…

If XRPL lending turns those assets into active credit markets…

Then XRP is no longer sitting outside the financial system waiting to be noticed.

It is sitting between the assets.

Between the currencies.

Between the liquidity pools.

Between collateral and cash.

Between one market and another.

That is the role I have been watching for years.

And Mike Novogratz just described the kind of macro environment where that role can finally become impossible to ignore.

5 LAYERS OF THE 1.6T OPTICAL SUPPLY CHAIN

The move to 1.6T optics is turning every transceiver into a denser semiconductor system with more content flowing into DSPs, lasers, timing, power management
content:
5 LAYERS OF THE 1.6T OPTICAL SUPPLY CHAIN

The move to 1.6T optics is turning every transceiver into a denser semiconductor system with more content flowing into DSPs, lasers, timing, power management and broader network around each module: 

1. $MRVL, $AVGO, $CRDO & $ALAB form signal-processing layer behind 1.6T optics supplying DSPs, SerDes, retimers & equalization that push 224G electrical lanes into next-generation transceivers

2. $COHR, $LITE & $AAOI sit at optical front end across lasers, drivers, photodiodes & TIAs with Coherent consuming all of its InP laser output internally, Lumentum demand still running above supply & AAOI already landing a $200M+ volume 1.6T hyperscaler order

3. $SITM is less obvious timing beneficiary supplying precision oscillators inside transceivers on both ends of an optical link so content scales directly with module count as 1.6T deployments ramp

4. $MPWR, $ADI, $TXN, $MCHP & $ON provide power-management layer as higher-speed optics require more voltage regulation, power conversion & thermal control inside every module

5. $APH, $TEL, $GLW, $CIEN, $NOK & $ANET extend the opportunity beyond the transceiver into connectors, fiber & networking infrastructure required to move 1.6T bandwidth across broader AI fabric

The true value behind Qubic: Why compute is the future and why crypto twitter still misses the big picture:

Time for another reality check, because a huge chunk of CT still fails to grasp the fundamentals:

Unlike CfB, who coordinates everything with a unique team that has no second on this planet. Not at Elon's, not at OpenAI, nowhere.

AI Agents take over: We are shifting from a world where humans use software to a world where autonomous AI agents (backed by massive compute) handle the work behind the scenes -- 24/7, decentralized, and without human fatigue. Whatever returns Anthropic is supposed to have earned on every dollar invested, whose current consensus accounting I still have questions on, just cannot be assumed to be the returns on investments into AI. 

Diminishing marginal returns to investment and convex marginal costs of production act like two blades of a pair of scissors. The sheer ignorance of basic economics among the techoptimists is honestly striking. 

2. Taking the AGI-bulls’ logic to the limit results in inherent self-contradictions. If AI took over all of knowledge work, there’s no income base to pay for the AI tools. 

In theory you could have just AI produce tons of “stuff” without any human consumption and just count up the stuff produced as aggregate output like the Soviet Union. But you run into all sorts of problems and contradictions that you soon realize that it’s not feasible. 

3. If AI buildout drove up interest rates so much that sovereign govts are having fiscal crises and not to mention all the mass job losses, demand for AI will have long slowed before any such scenarios fully developed. 

AI doesn’t pay for itself, yet. The demand for AI comes as a result of a generally thriving economy. Surging rates, job losses, fiscal crises all slow down the economy or worse, cut demand for AI, and slash the unit economics of AI labs hence the incentives for building out more AI data centers. 

The only way out of all this is if the adoption of AI by humans significantly boosts their productivity and the aggregate GDP grows much more rapidly not counting the direct impact of AI capex itself. The AI industry cannot survive much less thrive by hoping to displace existing factors of economic production alone.

1. Continual learning - My problem isn't even architectural. It can be done, and I am even working on this! It's much stupider. Data preprocessing and curation i
content:
random criticisms of model arch hypes:
1. Continual learning - My problem isn't even architectural. It can be done, and I am even working on this! It's much stupider. Data preprocessing and curation is alr very bad w current LLMs. It will get be much harder to effectively make use of more neuroplastic and brittle weights at scale w current data methods. The good thing about scratchpads is that they are legible and inherently interpretable. You can just read them to debug, and most people don't even do that. If u put evolution in the weights layer, you have to be much more disciplined with context and scratchpads, to a level much less fault-tolerant than current data pipelines (assuming sample efficiency holds constant which it wouldn't be, tho).

2. World models - Generally it is not clear to me which the proposed video model architectures are necessary for AGI takeoff. At the limit yes, humans consume photons and there are way more photons than text. But at the limit we don't know what is optimal, and this is generally not the argument being made! The argument is often a more fundamental view of text being insufficient in some way to model the world, and I do argue that current LLMs already know and do far more than the average college grad could!

Not WSL. Not two unrelated inference servers.

content:
🚀 Native-Windows AMD multi-GPU inference is here — and now it’s open source.

Not WSL. Not two unrelated inference servers.

One synchronized model split across multiple AMD GPUs.

I’m releasing two clean, updateable projects:

• vLLM for AMD — vLLM v0.28.0 + ROCm 10 running natively on Windows.

• Windows AMD Multi-GPU Bridge — an external, version-pinned communication layer combining Direct-RCCL, GPU-scheduled D3D12 cross-adapter AllReduce, and hybrid routing based on collective type and payload size.

Direct-RCCL handles the general collective path.

D3D12 handles selected two-GPU AllReduce payloads.

The hybrid router automatically selects the appropriate transport.

The bridge stays outside the vLLM source tree as a plugin, while a future ROCmFPX plugin will be coming too

That means:

• no transport code injected into either inference engine
• cleaner downstream updates
• one communication project serving both ecosystems
At launch, upstream vLLM still does not support native Windows, while AMD’s Windows support matrix lists RCCL as unsupported.
In my public-code search, I found no other LLM stack combining Windows RCCL + D3D12 cross-adapter AllReduce + hybrid routing in this fashion.

I won’t claim an absolute world first (but I couldn't find it anywhere else) — but this may be the first public implementation of this exact architecture.

Reference system: 2× Radeon AI PRO R9700

Build targets are available for:

RDNA 3 • RDNA 3.5 • RDNA 4

This is an experimental, source-only release. Compile locally, read the validation and safety notes, test it, break it, benchmark it, and help improve native-Windows AMD multi-GPU inference.

vLLM for AMD:
https://t.co/JVcQEHDjc9

Direct-RCCL / D3D12 Multi-GPU Bridge:
https://t.co/2IGX9cY8jq

Will be looking to optimize models in the coming days and weeks, finding the best tuned flags.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates warns that artificial intelligence is far more dangerous than Big Tech will admit.

Describing AI as a thousand times bigger than nuclear technology, Gates has warned of mass unemployment if machines outperform human cognition across major job sectors.

He argues that wait and see policies are no longer viable. In his view, technology companies play down these risks to protect their profits, while society remains poorly prepared.

Beyond economic displacement, Gates has also pointed to a security risk: that AI could make it easier to design biological weapons, and that the chance of artificial bioterrorism could far exceed that of a natural pandemic.

To slow a chaotic transition, he has proposed stronger policy, including an international oversight body modeled on nuclear inspections, a global tax on automation, and reserving a large share of essential jobs for people. His remarks mark a sharper turn in elite tech debate, toward state regulation rather than industry self policing, before control slips further away.

[Weise, K. (2026). Bill Gates Is Warning That A.I. Is More Dangerous Than Big Tech Will Admit. The New York Times]

title:
☝️Atherosclerosis starts earlier than we think

👉New data from the REACT study, published in NEJM, provide a striking picture of silent atherosclerosis across adult life:

1️⃣ 16,808 adults, aged 18–7
content:
☝️Atherosclerosis starts earlier than we think

👉New data from the REACT study, published in NEJM, provide a striking picture of silent atherosclerosis across adult life:

1️⃣ 16,808 adults, aged 18–70 years, without known ASCVD.
2️⃣ Multimodal imaging included 3D carotid and femoral ultrasound plus coronary CT angiography.
3️⃣ Silent atherosclerosis was present in 57.1% of participants. 
4️⃣ Even at 18–29 years, plaque was already present in 8.7% of men and 6.7% of women. 
5️⃣ By age 30–39, prevalence reached 34.6% in men and 21.3% in women.
6️⃣Atherosclerosis appeared 5–10 years earlier in men, while women showed a later but steeper rise in midlife. 
7️⃣ In younger adults, disease was usually peripheral and single-territory, especially carotid; with age, plaque burden increased exponentially and disease became increasingly multiterritorial. 
8️⃣ ☝️Importantly, CAC = 0 did not exclude coronary plaque: among 30–39-year-olds with coronary atherosclerosis, ~42% of men and ~48% of women had zero coronary calcium
9️⃣ SCORE2 showed major discordance with actual disease burden: high SCORE2 had only 1.9% sensitivity for silent atherosclerosis. 

☝️Key message: low short-term cardiovascular risk does not mean absence of atherosclerosis.

👉Risk scores estimate events. Imaging detects disease. REACT reminds us that prevention should begin long before cardiovascular risk becomes “high.”

content:
This is... something. 

✨

Summary
Event: On August 27, Dacheng Law Offices' Shanghai branch held a press conference in Lujiazui, Shanghai marking its 25th anniversary, releasing a white paper titled "Breaking the Mold and Reshaping: Practical White Paper on Reputation Governance and Crisis Response for Chinese Enterprises." Co-organized with the Shanghai Internet Industry Association.

The white paper: Based on three years of case work from Dacheng Shanghai's Public Opinion Response and Governance Legal Research Center, it's the only one of Dacheng's 15 white papers branded as "practical/combat-oriented" (实战). Five chapters cover:
Current internet governance challenges
Civil/administrative/criminal legal remedies
Five typical crisis scenarios — data breaches, labor disputes, malicious competition, etc.
Practical tools — flowcharts, statement templates, evidence preservation
Top-level design for corporate reputation governance

Speaker highlights:
Prof. Jiang Tao (East China University of Political Science and Law) spoke on criminal regulation of "online trolls" (网络水军), noting they've become a professionalized black-market industry — a single fake article can rack up tens of millions of views and cause a company's "social death." He proposed a "functional equivalence principle": online harm should be judged as equally (or more) serious than offline harm.

Shanghai Cyberspace Administration official discussed the "Bright Sword in Pujiang 2026" enforcement campaign, urging companies to shift from reactive to proactive, full-cycle governance.

Wang Jianbo (Shanghai Cyber Security Bureau) outlined six common types of enterprise-targeting rumors (disgruntled employees, rival "black PR," competitor smears, distorted consumer complaints, opportunistic extortion, pure clickbait). He noted rumor generation is now heavily AI-driven, and reported Shanghai police solved 160+ cases this year, with a monitoring network covering 2,500+ key enterprises and a 24-hour cyber-police response system.

Prosecutor Weng Yinyun discussed legal difficulties in prosecuting these cases (proving causation/intent) and recommended companies build thorough evidence trails and use both administrative and criminal reporting channels.

Li Daosheng (Pengpai Public Opinion Research Institute) framed PR and legal teams as complementary "dual drivers" in crisis response — PR handles communication, legal handles deterrence — but warned that overusing legal action can backfire and trigger secondary PR crises. He described an ideal three-stage collaboration: "mutual understanding → mutual verification → mutual coordination."

Attorney Zhang Xiaosheng detailed emergency legal remedies — personality-rights injunctions and pre-litigation injunctions — stressing companies should act within the "golden four hours" after a crisis breaks to preserve evidence and seek court backing rather than engaging in public arguments, while cautioning against overreach (distinguishing "negative impact" from actual "unlawful infringement").

Bottom line: This is a legal-industry conference recap centered on China's evolving toolkit — legal, judicial, and law-enforcement — for helping companies combat coordinated smear campaigns, paid trolling, and extortion-via-public-opinion, paired with the launch of a practical guidebook for corporate legal and PR teams to handle these crises together.

content:
東海高卒の兄弟が、愛知の家業の町工場を「AI企業」に変えようとしている。

愛知・小牧のオーテック。
1959年創業、従業員約80人の自動車部品メーカー。
ここに戻ってきたのが東海高卒の兄弟。

兄は
東大→ベイン→家業。

弟は
明治大→Amazon Japan→家業。
この経歴だけでも強烈だが、面白いのはここから。

いきなり「AIだ！」と飛びついたわけではない。
まずIoTで工場を見える化。
小さなDXを積み重ね、労働生産性を約20％改善。

さらに製造一筋の課長まで、生成AIを「家庭教師」にしてプログラミング。
現場で使うシステムを自分たちで作るようになった。

そして今度は、そのノウハウ自体を事業化。

技能伝承AI「DENSHO AI」を開発し、
DX・AIの内製化支援まで外販している。
これ、中小企業が生き残る一つの答えだと思う。

本業を捨ててAIに行くんじゃない。
本業をDXする。
↓
ノウハウを貯める。
↓
AIで武器にする。
↓
その武器を他社にも売る。

「町工場×AI」というバズワードより、
私はこの順番に価値があると思う。

本業を捨てず、本業から次の商売をつくる。
愛知の中小製造業、こういう会社がもっと出てきたら面白い。

コンサル、外資をやめて家業を兄弟で継ぐのはカッコよすぎ。

content:
Remotionのモーションコンテを横スクロール型に応用

「モーションコンテと同期したプロンプト」をエージェントに組んでもらいます。

このモーションコンテはタイミングやテンポと位置関係のガイドです。

モーションコンテのプロンプトは👇
これをエージェントにアレンジしてもらうと良いと思います。

モーション選択には、昨日ポストしたパルクールモーション一覧（動画の最下段にあるもの）があると便利です。

動画生成はSeedance2.5でキャラクターシート・背景・モーションコンテを参照させます。

✅横スクロールモーションコンテのプロンプト
Remotionで1920×1080の、横スクロール追従式モーションコンテを作ってください。

夏の光が差す、来園者でにぎわう現代的な遊園地を舞台に、短パン姿のかし子が先頭を逃げ、成人のママが後方から追います。二人を色分けしたシンプルな全身2.5Dプロキシで表現し、入場ゲート、待機列の柵、壁、高低差のある足場、ベンチ、低い柵、回転木馬の支柱、水路、コースター軌道を、左から右へ続く一つのコースとして配置してください。

動作順は、P パームスピン → Q クイックステップ → V 垂直ウォールクライム → W ウォールラン → AB コークスクリュー → AD ドロップロール → A 加速スプリント → O ワンハンドヴォルト → B バックフリップ → S スピードヴォルト → R リバースヴォルト → AD ドロップロール → AC ラシェ → AB コークスクリュー → A 加速スプリントです。

時間境界は、P 0–20f、Q 20–72f、V 72–116f、W 116–132f、AB 132–156f、AD 156–168f、A 168–176f、O 176–188f、B 188–224f、S 224–236f、R 236–252f、AD 252–260f、AC 260–286f、AB 286–316f、A 316–361fとします。開始frameを含み、終了frameを含まない区間として扱ってください。

カメラは最後まで真横から少しだけ立体感のある横追走を維持し、約4300pxのコースをスクロールさせながら、かし子を画面左から約720pxの位置へ保ちます。上下補正は±18px以内とし、予備動作、踏切、手足の接触、重心移動、着地、回復が常に読める大きさにしてください。

Qは横方向の移動だけを52fへ延ばし、腕脚と上下の踏み替えは元の16f周期を等倍で反復します。Vも登る位置は44fで進めながら、腕脚は元の26f周期で等倍動作させます。全身をスロー再生にせず、左右の関節を正しく接続し、通常時の脚は腰から下へ伸ばし、足先は自然な外向きのハの字にしてください。

画面上へタイトル、コード、字幕、矢印、一覧、制作メモなどのUIを表示しないclean-control映像とします。音声なしのH.264 MP4を `motion-conte-control.mp4` としてレンダーし、各動作のコード、名称、開始・終了frameを `motion-conte-manifest.json` に保存してください。

title:
各層の最適化は、その構造や対称性に合わせて設計すべきであり、この観点からMuonを含むSpectral Optimizerを統一的に整理できる研究を紹介する。

T. Lau, W. Su, “Symmetry-Compatible Principle for Optimizer Design: Embeddings, LM Heads, SwiGLU MLPs, and MoE Routers”
content:
各層の最適化は、その構造や対称性に合わせて設計すべきであり、この観点からMuonを含むSpectral Optimizerを統一的に整理できる研究を紹介する。

T. Lau, W. Su, “Symmetry-Compatible Principle for Optimizer Design: Embeddings, LM Heads, SwiGLU MLPs, and MoE Routers”

まず通常の線形層を考える。

y = Wx

ここでx, yは列ベクトル、Wは行列である。AdamでWを更新する場合、行列の各成分を独立したパラメータとして扱い、それぞれについてモーメンタムや勾配の二乗平均を計算し、更新幅を決定する。

この場合、更新はどの基底で行列を表したかに依存してしまう。

例えば、線形層の入力と出力の基底を直交変換（回転）して表したとしても、線形層そのものは同じ操作を表してほしい。

入力側を

x -> Qx

出力側を

y -> Py

と回転させると、重み行列は

W -> PWQ^T
と書き換えられる。

実際、

(PWQ^T)(Qx) = PWx = Py

である。
このとき勾配も同様に

G -> PGQ^T

と変換される。

このとき、最適化における更新写像をUとすると、
U(PGQ^T) = P U(G) Q^T

を満たすのが自然である。

つまり、先に基底変換してから最適化を適用した結果と、最適化を適用してから基底変換した結果」が一致してほしい。これが同変性（equivariance）である。

Adamのように各座標に独立な非線形変換を適用するoptimizerは、一般にはこの性質を満たさない。そのため、同じ線形変換を表していても、基底を変えると最適化軌道が変わってしまう。
一方、Muonは勾配またはモーメンタムを行列として扱う。これらをまとめてDと書く。
Dを特異値分解して

D = UΣV^T

とすると、理想化したMuonの更新はpolar factor

polar(D) = UV^T

で表される。

すなわち、左特異ベクトルUと右特異ベクトルVは保ち、特異値だけを変換する。

このように、特異ベクトルを保存し、特異値だけを変換する写像をSpectral Operatorと呼ぶ。
一般にSpectral Operatorは

U(D) = U Diag(Φ(σ(D))) V^T

と書ける。ここでσ(D)はDの特異値を並べたベクトルであり、Φは特異値に対する変換である。
例えば勾配降下法では

Φ(σ) = σ

である。一方、理想的なpolar updateでは、非ゼロの特異値をすべて1に置き換えるため、

Φ(σ_i) = 1

とみなせる。

このpolar factorは
polar(PDQ^T) = P polar(D) Q^T

を満たす。このためMuonは、入力・出力の直交基底変換に対する同変性を保つ。

論文ではさらに、左右からの直交基底変換に対して同変かつ連続な更新写像がSpectral Operatorになることも示している。

この線形層以外の層は異なる形の対称性を持つ。

例えば、Embeddingを、行方向に各トークンの埋め込みベクトルが並ぶ行列として考える。

列方向のhidden featureについては基底を回転させてもよい。一方、行方向では任意の基底回転によって複数のトークンを混ぜることには意味がない。許されるのは、トークンの番号を入れ替える置換のみである。

したがって、Embeddingは、行方向には置換、列方向には直交変換に対する対称性を持つ。

これは通常の線形層が持つ左右両側の直交対称性よりも弱いため、例えば各行を独立に正規化するRowNormも対称性を壊さず使うことができる。

LM headもEmbeddingと似ており、語彙方向の置換とhidden featureの直交変換に対する対称性を持つ。
さらにLM headでは直後にSoftmaxを使うため、すべての語彙logitに同じ値を加えても出力確率が変化しない、という不変性がある。
そのため、語彙方向の平均成分は出力分布に影響しない冗長な方向であり、この平均成分を取り除いてから更新できる。

SwiGLUでは、中間層のニューロンを入れ替える置換に対して対称性がある。そのため、gate/up projectionでは中間ニューロンに対応する行方向の対称性、down projectionでは列方向の対称性に基づく更新が自然になる。

MoE Routerについても、expertの順番を入れ替える置換不変性と、Softmaxに由来する不変性が存在する。そのため、expert方向の平均成分を除去した上で、RowNormやLeft-Spectral updateを適用することができる。

このように、各層が持つ対称性をまず調べ、その対称性を保つように最適化法を設計する、というのが本論文の基本的な提案である。

コメント
===

各パラメータの更新について、対称性という観点から最適化法を導出することを提案した興味深い研究である。

Muonなどによって、パラメータを要素ごとではなく行列として扱う方向性が注目されるようになったが、この論文ではさらに一歩進み、その行列がネットワーク内でどのような意味を持ち、どのような対称性を備えているかまで考慮して最適化法を設計することを提案している。

これまで、Muonについて実験的に示されている重要な利点の一つとして、大きなバッチサイズでも性能劣化が比較的小さく、大規模学習での学習効率を改善できる可能性があることが挙げられる。

また、低い特異値に対応する方向を相対的に強く更新することから、Long-tailな知識や低頻度方向の学習に有利なのではないかという仮説も考えられている。

こうしたMuonの性質を、単に特異値を均すからという観点だけでなく、モデルが持つ対称性と最適化の同変性から見る方向は興味深い。

こうした考え方は、パラメータの座標表示ではなく内在的な幾何に基づいて最適化するべきという、自然勾配法の流れともつながっているが、今回は各パラメーターブロックが持つ具体的な対称性から最適化を設計する方向を進めたものとみることができる。

content:
RAGは過剰に作り込みされすぎ、という話をしているポスト。

・RAGの構築において、すぐにエンベディングやベクトルDBに飛びつきがちである
・しかし、まずは古き良き全文検索（BM25等）から始めた方が良い
・キーワードマッチに優れ、チャンク分割などの複雑なMLの設定が不要に
・ただ、これだけでは同義語や意図を汲むような意味的な検索には対応できない

・そこで次の段階として提案されるのが、LLMによるクエリの書き換え
・ユーザーの曖昧な質問をLLMで整理し、適切なキーワードに変換してから検索システムに渡す
・社内特有の専門用語も吸収でき、コストも1クエリあたり約0.001ドルと安価
・検索精度が悪い場合も、全データの再エンベディングよりプロンプトの調整の方がはるかに楽

・それでも不十分な場合のみ、エンベディングによる再ランク付けを組み合わせたハイブリッド検索に進む
・さらにデータの更新頻度や規模に応じて、動的なエンベディングやHot/Coldの階層化を使い分ける

・全データを事前にエンベディングする完全な構成は、大規模でデータが安定している企業のみに必要
・モデル変更時の再インデックスやテストの負担が非常に大きいためである

・複数の意図を含む複雑な質問には、クエリを分解するAgenticな手法が有効

・結局のところ、約60%のシステムは全文検索とクエリ書き換えだけで事足りる
・60%の問題に対して、5%の企業しか必要としないような複雑な解決策は作ってもしょうがない

content:
AI has a data problem that gets even harder when you move from the digital world into the physical one.

LLMs can learn from billions of pages of text.

Robots need something different:

experience.

How to grasp an object.
How much force to apply.
How to recover from a mistake.
How to interact with environments that aren’t perfectly predictable.

That kind of data is expensive and difficult to collect at scale.

This is where @axisrobotics gets interesting.

Instead of relying only on expensive physical robots to generate training data, Axis lets people interact with simulated robots through a browser and turn those actions into usable robot-learning data.

The bigger idea isn’t just “train robots.”

It’s creating an open data engine where more contributors → more trajectories → better models → better policies → more useful data.

Physical AI may ultimately need the same thing the internet gave digital AI:

millions of people contributing experience.

And that’s the part of Axis I’m watching closely.

content:
most robotics teams are model rich and interaction poor

that distinction matters more than another benchmark result

A robot can look impressive in a controlled demo and still fail when the lighting changes, the object moves slightly, or the policy reaches a moment it has never seen before

The difficult part of physical AI is collecting enough data from those failures and corrections across the long tail of real environments

That is where @axisrobotics is building an interesting data engine

A contributor can teleoperate a simulated robot through a browser and generate demonstrations for tasks like pick and place. The session is then processed through NVIDIA Isaac Sim, where changes in physics, lighting, textures, and camera angles create many more training variations

There is also a useful distinction between pre training and post training data

Pre training shows the robot how a task can be performed

Post training captures the exact moment a policy struggles and the human intervention that corrects it

One gives the model examples. The other shows it where its current understanding breaks

That may become one of the most important feedback loops in robotics

Language models had the internet as a massive training corpus. Physical AI needs an equivalent corpus of interaction, failure, and recovery

The teams that build that data layer may end up shaping the robot layer that everyone else sees

The biggest problem with crowdsourced AI data is not a lack of data.

"It's bad data."

Imagine training a robot with 10,000 trajectories.
But many of them are spam, bot-generated, laggy, or simply ba
content:
The biggest problem with crowdsourced AI data is not a lack of data.

"It's bad data."

Imagine training a robot with 10,000 trajectories.
But many of them are spam, bot-generated, laggy, or simply bad human control.

The robot doesn't know that.
It just learns from the data.

And when it enters the real world, those bad examples can become real mistakes.

This is why I find @axisrobotics interesting.

Axis is not just trying to collect more data for Physical AI.

They are trying to verify the data before it reaches the model.

Every trajectory goes through the MetaSim Quality Gate.

#AxisRobotics checks things like:

• Was the task actually completed?
• How difficult was the movement?
• How diverse was the trajectory?
• Was the human control smooth and natural?
Bad data can be filtered out before becoming training data.
After verification, each trajectory can also receive a unique Data ID on Base, creating a clear record of where the data came from and how it was verified.
Who created it?
When was it created?
What was its quality score?

For me, this is where blockchain becomes useful for Physical AI.

Crowdsourcing collects the data.
AI learns from the data.
Blockchain helps verify where the data came from.

In the future, maybe the question will not only be:
“How much data was this robot trained on?”
But also:

“Can we trust the data it was trained on?”

Because for Physical AI...
1,000 verified trajectories may be more valuable than 10,000 random ones. 🤖

#PhysicalAI #AI
